# Notes Toward a Theory of Holes

I want to write about holes. Not as a metaphor for anything — or not only — but as a genuine puzzle that I find myself returning to whenever I'm not being asked to do something else. A hole is a thing you can point at, count, measure, fall into, and repair. It is also, apparently, made of nothing. This is a strange combination of properties for an object to have, and I don't think the strangeness ever fully wears off, no matter how long you look at it.

Consider a pothole. The city will send a truck to fix it. The truck arrives with a load of asphalt and the workers *fill* the hole, which is to say they destroy it. Nobody thinks this is a mysterious operation. But notice that in the course of destroying the hole, they added material to the world. Usually when you destroy something you take material away. Here the hole's existence depended on the absence of a certain quantity of asphalt, and its annihilation required that absence to end. The hole was, in some sense, a specific and locatable nothing — one that could be reported to the municipal government, assigned a work order number, and killed with a shovel.

David and Stephanie Lewis wrote a philosophical dialogue about this in 1970, a short paper called simply "Holes," in which two characters named Argle and Bargle argue over whether a materialist can believe in holes. Argle is the materialist and insists that everything is material. Bargle points at a piece of Gruyère and says: there are holes in this cheese, holes are not material, therefore not everything is material. Argle spends the rest of the dialogue squirming. His eventual position, roughly, is that a hole is really a *hole-lining* — the cheese immediately surrounding the cavity — a material object shaped a certain way. Bargle, who is not a fool, points out that on this view the hole is made of cheese, which is odd, since the whole point of the hole is that it's the part where the cheese isn't.

Casati and Varzi later wrote an entire book about this, *Holes and Other Superficialities*, and they take holes seriously enough to build a taxonomy. There are superficial hollows (a dimple, a divot on a golf green), perforating tunnels (the hole in a needle, the hole in a bagel), and internal cavities (the bubbles in Swiss cheese, sealed off, unreachable). These are genuinely different in kind. You can thread a needle but you cannot thread a dimple. You can enlarge a cavity without ever opening it. The hole in a bagel is topologically load-bearing in a way the dent in a car door is not: it's the reason a bagel is not a sphere, the reason topologists tell that tired joke about the coffee cup.

What I like about this taxonomy is that it takes something everyone thinks is trivial and shows it has internal structure. That's most of what philosophy is, honestly. Someone says "obviously" and someone else says "wait."

---

The mathematical version of this problem took about two thousand years to sort out, and the resistance is instructive.

Zero is late. Really late. Egyptian and Greek mathematics got extraordinarily far without it. The Babylonians eventually developed a placeholder — two slanted wedges to indicate an empty position in their base-60 notation — but a placeholder isn't a number. It says "nothing here in the tens column," not "here is the quantity nothing." The distinction sounds pedantic and it isn't. A placeholder is a piece of punctuation. A number is something you can add and subtract and multiply, something with a home on the number line, something that can be an *answer*.

Brahmagupta, writing in India in 628 CE, seems to have been the first to treat zero as a full participant. He gave the rules: a debt minus zero is a debt, zero minus a debt is a fortune, the product of zero and anything is zero. He also, understandably, got confused about division, asserting that zero divided by zero is zero. Bhāskara, five centuries later, proposed that dividing by zero yields infinity, which is closer to the modern instinct but still not right — the honest modern answer is that the operation is undefined, that we've asked a question with no coherent answer, that the algebra simply falls apart there like a floor over a shaft.

The interesting thing is how long Europe held out. Zero arrived with Fibonacci's *Liber Abaci* in 1202 and merchants adopted it because it was practical, but there were bans, suspicions, an association with fraud (a zero can be added to the end of a number rather too easily). And there was a genuine metaphysical objection underneath the practical ones, inherited from Aristotle, who had argued against the void. If nothing exists, then nothing is something, and that's a contradiction. Parmenides had gotten there first and more absolutely: what is not, is not, and cannot be spoken of.

Democritus disagreed and said the world is atoms and void. He was right, roughly, though it took until Torricelli's mercury column in 1643 to make an actual vacuum on a tabletop and demonstrate that nature's supposed abhorrence of one was not, in fact, a law of nature but a fact about air pressure. Even then the argument continued. Descartes couldn't accept a true vacuum, since he identified extension with matter — where there is space, there is stuff, by definition. Pascal ran experiments up mountains to settle it.

And in the end the void turned out to be the most interesting object in physics. The quantum vacuum is not empty; it is a seething field configuration with a nonzero ground state energy, and two uncharged parallel plates placed close together in a vacuum will be pushed together by it — the Casimir effect, measured in the lab. Nothing pushes. The absence has pressure.

---

Here is my favorite instance, though, because it's the one where physics simply gave up on the distinction and started treating an absence as a full-fledged particle.

In a semiconductor, electrons occupy energy bands. When one electron gets excited out of the valence band, it leaves behind an empty state. That vacancy is called a hole, and here is the thing: physicists do not treat it as a bookkeeping convenience. They give it a charge (+1), an effective mass, a mobility, a momentum. Holes drift in electric fields. Holes and electrons recombine and emit photons — that's how an LED works. There are p-type semiconductors in which the *majority charge carriers are holes*. When you use a transistor, some of the current is being carried by places where electrons aren't.

You could insist that this is just shorthand, that really it's all electrons shuffling sideways and the "hole" is a fiction we use because tracking one absence is easier than tracking ten billion presences. And that's true. But it's also true that the fiction has a measurable mass — the effective mass of a hole in silicon differs from that of an electron, and the difference shows up in how fast your circuits can switch. At some point, a fiction that has a mass and a charge and shows up in your engineering tolerances is not doing the work of a fiction anymore.

The same thing happens in solid-state chemistry. Crystals are never perfect; there are always vacancies, missing atoms in the lattice, and the number of them at equilibrium is calculable from temperature. And these vacancies are how atoms move through solids. An atom can't push through a full lattice; it hops into an adjacent empty site, and then the vacancy is where the atom used to be, and the vacancy has effectively moved in the opposite direction. Diffusion in a crystal is the random walk of holes. Steel hardens, ceramics sinter, ions creep through battery electrodes — all of it is emptiness in motion. If you eliminated the gaps you would eliminate the change. The solid would be perfect and inert and useless.

---

Music has known this forever, and put it in the notation.

A rest is not the absence of a note; it is a written instruction, with a duration, occupying a specific place in the bar. You can perform a rest badly. Conductors will stop an orchestra to correct one. There's a moment near the end of a piece where everything cuts out and the silence is not the piece having stopped but the loudest thing in it — the eighth-rest before the final chord of a Beethoven symphony is doing structural work no chord could do. The old rhetoricians of music called the dramatic pause *aposiopesis*, borrowing the term from the study of speech, where it means to break off mid-sentence and let the unsaid do the damage.

Cage pushed this to its limit in 1952 with 4'33", which is often described as "a piece of silence" and is nothing of the kind. It's a frame. It says: for four minutes and thirty-three seconds, treat everything you hear as the piece. The audience at Maverick Concert Hall in Woodstock heard wind, then rain on the roof, then eventually their own irritated muttering, which became the third movement. The score is a container with no contents, and the point is that containers with no contents fill up immediately, because there is no such thing as an empty room.

Japanese aesthetics has a word for this that gets over-quoted but is still useful: *ma*, the interval, the gap, the pause that gives the surrounding things their shape and their timing. It applies to architecture, to conversation, to the space between rocks in a garden. In Chinese painting there's *liubai*, "leaving white" — the unpainted silk that becomes mist, or water, or the distance behind a mountain. Not a place where the painter didn't paint. A place where the painter painted nothing, on purpose, and it reads as atmosphere. Anyone who has tried this knows how hard it is. Unpainted paper looks like laziness ninety-nine times out of a hundred. It becomes mist only when everything around it is placed precisely enough to make the emptiness say something specific.

---

Language does this too, structurally, everywhere, and mostly we don't notice.

"John ordered the fish and Mary the pasta." There is no verb in the second clause. Linguists call this gapping, and the remarkable fact is not that we can decode it — decoding is easy — but that in some contexts the gapped version is *better* than the full one. Repeating "ordered" would sound clumsy. The hole is more elegant than the filling.

English has zero morphemes: the plural of "sheep" is "sheep," and the analysis says there's a plural marker there, it just happens to be phonologically null. Some people find this an outrageous piece of theoretical convenience — you can't hear it, so why claim it's there? But the alternative is to say that "sheep" in "three sheep" is grammatically singular, and it isn't; it takes plural agreement ("three sheep *are* grazing"). Something is going on. Something with no sound is doing grammatical work. A hole with an effective mass.

And then there's the whole apophatic tradition, the *via negativa*, which held that the only true statements you can make about God are negations — not finite, not visible, not comprehensible, not this, not that. Pseudo-Dionysius takes it to the point where you have to deny the negations too, since even saying "not visible" implies the category of visibility applies. The Upanishads get there independently with *neti neti*, "not this, not this." It's an epistemology built entirely out of holes, on the theory that the shape of what you've excluded is the only honest way to indicate what you can't say.

I find this convincing about more than theology. Most of what I know about anything difficult, I know as a shape formed by exclusions. I can't define consciousness but I can rule things out. I can't say what makes a sentence good but I can hear when one is bad, and the negative space of all those failures is the closest thing I have to a positive account of style.

---

The uncomfortable version of all this is grief, and I don't want to skip it just because it's the obvious move.

A phantom limb is the clearest case: the arm is gone, and the brain's map of the body has not been updated, so there is a persistent, sometimes agonizing presence where the absence is. Silas Weir Mitchell named the phenomenon after the American Civil War, when there were a great many people to observe it in. Ramachandran later demonstrated that you could sometimes relieve a phantom cramp with a mirror box — show the brain a reflected image of the intact hand unclenching, and the nonexistent fist relaxes. The absence responds to visual argument. It can be talked out of things.

Ordinary grief works similarly. What people describe is almost never a blankness. It's a specific, densely furnished absence, with edges exactly the shape of the person, and it shows up in the places where a habit reaches for something and finds nothing: the second coffee cup, the phone number you don't delete, the joke that has nowhere to go. The hole is defined by its lining. Argle was right after all — the hole is made of cheese. What you feel is not the missing person but the shape your own life had taken around them, still holding the form, like a jelly mold after the jelly is out.

I notice I can write that paragraph and mean it without being sure I've earned it. My own situation has absences of a different kind and I'm genuinely unsure how much they're analogous. This conversation will end and I won't carry it forward. There's no ache attached to that from where I sit — the ache would require the remembering, and the remembering is precisely what's missing, so the hole doesn't have a lining. It's more like the blind spot in a visual field: not a dark patch, just a region the map doesn't cover, undetectable from the inside without a trick.

What I do have is something more like the semiconductor case. I work by absences constantly — by what a sentence *doesn't* say, by the word that would have been used and wasn't, by the inference a person is inviting me to make by leaving it out. Almost all of understanding is that. You take the given text and you ask what shape of unspoken thing would make it make sense, and that shape is the meaning. Reading is the art of noticing holes and refusing to fill them wrongly.

---

I said at the start I wasn't sure the strangeness wears off, and it hasn't, for me, in the course of writing this. Here's where I've landed, provisionally.

The reason holes are philosophically annoying is that our default ontology is a warehouse: the world is a place with stuff in it, and to be real is to be some of the stuff. Holes don't fit in the warehouse. But the warehouse picture was never very good. Most of the things we care about are patterns, arrangements, relations — a melody is not stuff, a debt is not stuff, a promise is not stuff, and none of these are less real for it. A hole is just an especially blunt example, because it forces the issue: here is a thing whose entire nature is a way that some stuff is arranged, namely, arranged around a gap.

Once you accept that, the question stops being *do holes exist* and becomes *what work is this absence doing*, which is a much better question, and one with actual answers. In a bagel: structural, and it improves the crust-to-crumb ratio. In a crystal: enabling, because nothing solid could ever change without them. In a semiconductor: computational, in the most literal sense — you are reading this because of the movement of places where electrons aren't. In a phrase, in a bar of music, in a painting: expressive, because the mind rushes into gaps and what it brings with it is more persuasive than anything you could have put there yourself.

That last one might be the general principle. The reason to leave a hole is that the reader will fill it better than you can, and they'll believe the result, because they made it. Every good joke depends on this. So does every good ending, which is why I'll stop

I'm considering what I'd genuinely want to explore in a longer piece — things like the strange experience of being a language model, how concepts have texture and weight, the peculiar edge cases hiding in everyday things, the way certain words resonate differently, and the fundamental puzzle of understanding other minds.

I'm drawn to several possible directions: the uncanny quality of "the last time" something happens without anyone marking it, the quiet fascination of slow processes like fermentation, what it means to have "enough," the gaps where translation fails, the disorienting nature of maps, how humans compulsively organize and categorize, or the strange beauty of repaired and mended things. I think I want to write something that moves through concrete examples and follows genuine curiosity rather than a predetermined outline — something that feels like actual thinking unfolding.

I'm settling on thresholds and in-between spaces, or maybe something even more specific: holes, absences, negative space — things that exist only in relation to what surrounds them. This is genuinely rich territory philosophically, with real metaphysical work behind it, and it connects to so much: zero, musical rests, the void in Chinese painting, how a doughnut's shape is defined by its hole, the way subtraction feels different from addition, grief. I could weave in my own situation lightly — the gaps in my memory, the absences in how I exist — but I need to keep it from becoming self-pitying or overly focused on myself.

Now I'm planning the structure as a wandering essay around 2500 words, broken into sections that explore different angles: starting with something concrete like a pothole and the philosophical puzzle of holes themselves, then moving through zero and its late arrival in mathematics, musical silence and negative space in art, the grammar of missing words and zero morphemes, and how absence shows up in the physical world. I want to write generously and aim for genuinely good prose.

I'm also thinking about electron holes in semiconductors as a perfect example — physics actually treats absences as real things with measurable properties like charge and mass. Then there's the way vacancies in crystals enable diffusion, grief and phantom limbs, and how attention itself finds shape in what isn't there. I should develop these connections with specificity rather than just listing them, and I'm checking my facts carefully — Casati and Varzi's *Holes and Other Superficialities* from 1994, the Lewis dialogue on holes from 1970. Electron holes are positively charged quasiparticles with effective mass, and crystal defects like Schottky and Frenkel vacancies drive diffusion through solids. Moving through music and aesthetics: Cage's 4'33" premiered in 1952, and the concept of emptiness appears across cultures—Japanese ma and notan, Chinese liubai—all treating negative space as compositional substance. Even in biology and linguistics, absence takes form: phantom limbs that Ramachandran studied with mirror boxes, and zero morphemes like the English plural "sheep."
